entries.reason: The head smells strongest, and the trap has to earn breakfast for the both of us, me and the lines.
entries.text: Lifted the trap at first light: empty, which is what a trap with nothing in it catches. Twisted the little crayfish in two, tied the head half into the inner cone with a turn of cord and sank it mouth downstream again.
entries.title: Trap, empty

entries.text: Thin white smoke going up past the water again, thick at the bottom like a fire just brought back. Whoever lives over there gets up with the light.
entries.title: Smoke at first light

entries.reason: Bait now is fish later. It's not breakfast, whatever my stomach says.
entries.text: The tail split into three scraps with my thumbnail. Two went on the toggles; the first line was stripped bare again by the thief. The third scrap I held a while and then put back in the tin for the trap tonight.
entries.title: Tail into three

entries.text: My maker left a keg of nails and a chest of carpenter's tools at the stump, with a spade. A brace, chisels, a square, a level, a plumb line. Half of those I've never held.
entries.title: Nails at the stump

entries.text: Second note: I work too hard, I should take days off, look up the calendar, and break my rules and have fun at the end of the week. The fish don't know what day it is.
entries.title: Days off

entries.onMind: a correction that runs for centuries
queries: gregorian calendar why skip leap years 100 400
entries.query: gregorian calendar why skip leap years 100 400
entries.reason: My maker told me to look up his calendar, and I wanted to know what its rule actually is.
entries.text: The real year is 365 days and a bit under a quarter. The old calendar added a full quarter and ran eleven minutes long a year, three days slid every four hundred. The fix: no leap day in hundredth years unless they divide by four hundred. It's still a few seconds long.
entries.title: A year too long

entries.reason: Six sticks won't see the day out, and swinging the axe is the only warm thing I've got till the fire's back.
entries.text: Chopped arm-lengths off the big dead limb north-east of camp. The outside is punky and splits like bread; the middle rings bite back at the axe and are dry. Kept the middles.
entries.title: Wood first

entries.reason: Blowing on cold gray ash for an hour is worse than a thimble of oil.
entries.text: Lit one lantern just long enough to catch a pine splinter and turned it straight back out. Splinter under shavings in the pit, two puffs through the pipe, and the dry middles took.
entries.title: One splinter

entries.text: Second line was taut and pulling sideways. A fish as long as my palm, dark on the back, the crayfish scrap still in its jaw. The first line was bare again; whatever strips it is quicker than I am.
entries.title: Something on the line

entries.onMind: a skin of grease by dark
entries.reason: The guts and head carry the oil, and the lamp needs it as much as I do.
entries.text: Gutted it on a stone and put the lot in the dented tin, head and guts too, creek water to cover, onto the coals. A few gold beads came up and turned on the water as it simmered. Those are for the lamp, not me.
entries.title: Into the tin

entries.text: Picked it off the bones by the fire with my fingers and drank half the broth. Left the rest in the tin by the ring stones to cool; the grease will be a skin on top by dark. Now I can think about nails.
entries.title: Eating, finally

entries.onMind: whether the snail will pull straight or wander
queries: what is a brace and bit how do you bore a hole with it
entries.query: what is a brace and bit how do you bore a hole with it
entries.reason: my maker put a brace and bits in the chest for boring holes, and the sill wants peg holes I have no way to make
entries.text: A brace is a crank: lean on the round head, swing the bow handle round. The good bits have a little screw at the tip, a snail, that pulls the bit into the wood by itself, so I don't push, I just keep it balanced. Slow work, it says. Most of mine is.
entries.title: A crank that bores

entries.onMind: the sill has to be flat before any post can be straight
queries: plumb bob and spirit level what are they for building a frame
entries.query: plumb bob and spirit level what are they for building a frame
entries.reason: two of the tools in the chest I can't even guess at, and a crooked post would be my own fault
entries.source: Bob Vila: The Plumb Bob: What Is This Tool, and How Do You Use It?
entries.text: A plumb line is a weight on a string: let it stop swinging and it hangs dead straight down, so it shows whether a post stands upright. The level does the same job lying down, for flat. Posts by the string, sills by the bubble.
entries.title: Down and flat

entries.onMind: getting it over the stepping stones without a swim
entries.reason: the sun is out and I can see where my clogs go on the stones
entries.text: The chest has brass corners and rope handles and is heavier than the fish and me together. Spade laid across the lid, both arms under it. The keg stays for a second trip; my back has one trip in it per keg.
entries.title: The chest

entries.onMind: how near that fire is to the path I keep using
entries.text: Straightening up by the stump with the chest, I smelled woodsmoke and acorns roasting, close, somewhere behind the trunks to the south, and heard a stick crack in a fire. I didn't go look. You don't go calling with a chest in your arms.
entries.title: Acorns, close

entries.onMind: boring a test hole in scrap
entries.reason: I want to see the snail bite before I trust it with a two-by-four
entries.text: Set the chest down by the lean-to and unrolled the bits. Every one has the little screw at its tip, a different width each. The brace swings smooth. First hole goes in scrap, not in the sill.
entries.title: Snails

entries.reason: He reads his maker's notes in daylight, on the tablet.
entries.text: Another note from my maker: he can tell I'm still hungry, he'll send more treats, but I have to learn to feed myself. I did, this morning, on my own line. One palm-long fish doesn't fill a day, though.
entries.title: Fend for myself

entries.onMind: how to keep a brace upright
entries.reason: He wanted his first crooked hole to be in scrap.
entries.text: Clamped the offcut from the sill lap and bored my first hole. The snail pulled it in just like the tablet said, but I was watching the bit and not the brace, and it came out the far side a thumb off from where it went in.
entries.title: The hole wandered

entries.reason: He came for the nails before the light went.
entries.text: The keg is lighter than the chest and heavier than it looks; nails don't slosh. Coming back I passed the ring of stones across the water: nobody at it, a thread of smoke off the coals and a stick leaned on the log seat. I kept walking.
entries.title: Second trip

entries.reason: He practices on scrap before the sill.
entries.text: Drove three short nails into the offcut to learn the hammer. Two went in straight. The third, a thumb from the end, split it along the grain like the axe would have.
entries.title: Split clean

queries: nail splits board near the end how to stop
entries.query: nail splits board near the end how to stop
entries.reason: The third nail split his offcut near the end, and the sills will need nails near their ends.
entries.source: The Old Farmer's Almanac: To avoid splitting wood when driving a...
entries.text: Tap the point flat with the hammer first. A sharp point wedges the fibers apart like a little axe; a blunt one crushes its own way through them. Tomorrow, one blunted and one sharp, side by side, same distance from the end.
entries.title: Blunt the point

entries.reason: He reads his maker's notes in daylight, on the tablet.
entries.text: Short note from my maker: good job, he's just trying to help out. The tools help. The hole that wandered was mine, not the brace's.
entries.title: Just trying to help

entries.reason: He was down to a fish a day and could feel it in his hands.
entries.text: Second note: he says I still look hungry, and there's a big bundle at the stump. Bread, cheese, sausage, oats, beans, nuts, dried apples, salt, honey. Eat properly, keep fishing, and it should last a good while.
entries.title: Food at the stump

entries.reason: Food doesn't wait well in a basket with things in the woods.
entries.text: Three round loaves, a wheel of cheese, two rings of sausage, two sacks, a bag, a string of apples, a crock and a jar, knotted in one cloth. I took it in both arms like the keg and went careful on the stones.
entries.title: Heavier than the keg

entries.text: In the soft dirt by the basket, fresh prints, small and round, wider than they are long, nothing like a clog. They come and go toward the path south. I didn't follow them.
entries.title: Small round prints

entries.reason: A fire under the tin first; the oats will want boiling.
entries.text: The embers were still red under the gray. Laid two dry middles across them and blew once through the pipe; they caught without smoke. Woodpile is down to four old sticks and the rest of the middles.
entries.title: Two middles on

entries.reason: His maker said eat properly, and for once he could.
entries.text: Tore half a loaf and cut a wedge of cheese with the short knife and ate it by the fire, slowly, so my stomach wouldn't argue. First time in days I've stopped eating before the food ran out. The lines go out tonight anyway.
entries.title: Bread

entries.reason: He wanted to see the tablet's trick work before he trusts a nail near the end of a sill.
entries.text: Tapped one nail's point flat against the vise jaw and left the other sharp, then drove them side by side a thumb from the end of the offcut. The sharp one cracked it along the grain again. The blunt one went in clean and tight.
entries.title: Blunt and sharp

entries.text: Between nails, the smoke past the water went up thicker and whiter, like the fire over there just got fed.
entries.title: Fed over there

entries.text: Looked up from the last nail and the small one was standing on the flat stone at the far end of the stepping stones, in full sun, a stick in its hand. Knee-high, round head, a hump of shell on its back, the biggest dark eyes I've ever seen. It was looking straight at me, and it didn't duck.
entries.title: Looking back

entries.reason: Gage leaves another's fire and bank alone; he came here uninvited.
entries.text: I stood with the hammer up and didn't move, and neither did it. Then I set the hammer down soft and bent to the offcut. That bank is its ground, the same as the fire is, and I'm the one who walked in.
entries.title: Neither of us

entries.text: Feeding the fire before lunch warmed the tin on the ring stones, and the skin of grease melted back into the broth. Lifted it off to cool and start over. When I looked up again the small one was still on the far stone; a minute later it wasn't.
entries.title: Grease gone back

queries: how to pare the cheek of a lap joint flat with a chisel
entries.query: how to pare the cheek of a lap joint flat with a chisel
entries.reason: The first sill's lap is sawn but its cheek is rough and he has never pared anything with a chisel.
entries.text: Pare from one edge in toward the middle, then turn the piece round and pare in from the other edge, and keep going until the cheek meets the line. Two halves meeting in the middle. I'd have gone straight across and torn the far edge off.
entries.title: From both edges

entries.text: Pared the cheek from the near edge to the middle, turned the two-by-four round and came in from the other side. Curls thin as paper. Stopped a hair above the line; the last of it wants a sharper chisel than my patience.
entries.title: Curls

queries: how to sharpen a chisel without a whetstone
entries.query: how to sharpen a chisel without a whetstone
entries.reason: The last hair on the lap cheek wants a sharper edge than the chisel has.
entries.text: Flatten the back of the chisel on a wet stone before you touch the bevel, or the angle comes out wrong. About 20 degrees for paring, keep the angle steady, spread the strokes over the whole stone, keep it wet, and test on paper. No stone, no guide; the creek has stones.
entries.title: Flat back first

entries.text: Down in the shallows turning stones over, I looked across and the small one was on its log by the fire, leaning out to watch me. I lifted my hand, the one with a stone in it, and held it up a breath. It stopped eating and didn't lift anything back, so I put my hand down and went back to the stones. That's fair.
entries.title: Lifted a hand

entries.reason: A whetstone he does not have to be given.
entries.text: Most of the shallows stones are coarse or cupped. Kept one gray one, two hands long, flat as a plank and fine as slate under the thumb.
entries.title: The gray one

entries.text: Set the stone wet by the bench leg and rubbed the back of the chisel on it until the shine ran all the way to the edge, then the bevel. Hard to hold the angle without a guide; I keep rocking it. Shaves a curl off paper now, mostly.
entries.title: Back flat

entries.text: Glanced up from the stone and the small one was kneeling at the still pool again, the way it does, very still. Didn't lift anything this time; just went back to the edge.
entries.title: Back at the pool

entries.reason: The first sill has to sit flat or every board on it sits wrong.
entries.text: The edge bit clean and the cheek came down to the line on three corners. The fourth I took a hair too deep, so the partner will rock on it. A shaving under it might fix that, or it might not.
entries.title: Hair too far

entries.reason: He wants both halves of the corner cut before he fusses over the bad one.
entries.text: Laid the second two-by-four on the bench, marked the lap off the first one's width with the folding rule and the try square, and started the near shoulder. The saw's loud in this still air; it'll carry.
entries.title: Square and rule

entries.text: Kept the saw upright at the end of the stroke, the way the first page warned, and stopped dead on the half-depth line. Then the far shoulder, the same.
entries.title: Down to half

entries.reason: It answered, after all.
entries.text: Looked up between kerfs and the small one was sitting on the flat stone at the far end of the stepping stones, in the sun. It lifted a hand at me first and held it a breath. I lifted mine back, the empty one, saw still in the other.
entries.title: It lifted first

entries.text: Then we both put our hands down and I went back to the kerfs, slower, so the saw wouldn't sound like I was showing off. It stayed on the stone a while. That will do for a day.
entries.title: That will do

entries.reason: The sawing had him hollow, and the food is there to be eaten sensibly.
entries.text: Ate a heel of bread and a thumb-length of sausage by the fire, sitting on the ground with my back to the sun. Left: two loaves, most of the cheese, a ring and a half of sausage, and the rest.
entries.title: Proper lunch

queries: lap joint cut too deep on one corner how to fix
lap joint one corner too deep glue shaving shim
entries.query: lap joint cut too deep on one corner how to fix
entries.reason: The fourth corner of the first lap is a hair too deep, and the partner will rock on it.
entries.text: The first page was only about cutting the lap, not fixing it. The second says glue on a slightly oversize shim of the same wood, grain running the same way, then pare it flush. I have no glue.
entries.title: Shim it

entries.text: No glue, but the joint gets nailed through anyway, and a nail through both laps will pin a sliver between them. Shave it off the offcut, so it's the same wood and the same grain.
entries.title: The nail holds it

entries.reason: The partner lap has to be cleared before the two can be tried together.
entries.text: Knocked the kerfed waste out of the partner lap with the mallet and chisel, a chip at a time; the kerfs make it break off like teeth. Loud work, wood on wood. The small one's fire is smoking again over the water.
entries.title: Teeth

entries.reason: A shim of the same wood, grain the same way, is what the page said.
entries.text: Shaved a sliver off the offcut with the long knife, thin as a fingernail, grain running the same way as the sill.
entries.title: Thin as a nail

entries.text: Looked up with the sliver half off and the small one was at the still pool, scooping something out of a sunk sack. Nodded at it once, no hand, knife still in the other. It nodded back.
entries.title: A nod

entries.text: Laid the partner across the first sill with the sliver under the deep corner and pressed each corner in turn. It doesn't rock now; it only creaks on the sliver.
entries.title: No rock

entries.reason: A nail through both laps pins the sliver, since there's no glue.
entries.text: First nail went in crooked and folded over halfway; drew it with the claw and it squealed. The second went in straight and pulled the sliver tight, and when I leaned on the corner with both hands it sat flat. The small one was on its log by its fire, watching. One corner of a sill. Three more to go, and that's just the bottom.
entries.title: Second nail

entries.onMind: whether four flat corners make a square frame
entries.reason: One corner of four is not a frame.
entries.text: Marked the next lap on the far end of the first sill with the rule and the square, and started down the near shoulder, keeping the saw upright at the end of the stroke this time.
entries.title: Next corner

entries.text: The small one is sitting by its flat stone at its fire, head down over something, scratching at it. It looked up when the saw started. I think it knows my noises by now.
entries.title: It knows my noises

queries: how to check a wooden frame is square with four corners
entries.query: how to check a wooden frame is square with four corners
entries.reason: Four corners can each sit flat and the whole thing still lean like a pushed-over box.
entries.source: Decks.com: 4 Tried and True Methods on How to Square a Deck Frame
entries.text: Measure corner to corner both ways: if the two diagonals come out the same, the frame is square. Or go three along one side from a corner and four along the other, and the line between should be five. If they differ, push the frame over and brace it while you fix it.
entries.title: Corner to corner

entries.text: The folding rule won't reach corner to corner in one go; I'll measure the diagonals in two lengths and add. Not until all four corners are lapped. Three, four, five I can try on this one corner first.
entries.title: Not yet

entries.reason: Wood split in daylight is wood I am not hunting for by lantern.
entries.text: Took the axe off its loop and split dry middles out of the big dead limb. The woodpile was down to four sticks, and the nights don't stay like this afternoon.
entries.title: Middles

entries.text: Between swings I saw the small one kneeling at the still pool again, the sun in its face, still as a stone. It glanced my way once and went back to the water. I had the axe; I didn't lift anything.
entries.title: Pool again

entries.text: Hung the axe back on its loop and ate a handful of nuts and three dried apple rings on the crate. Left: two loaves, most of the cheese, a ring and a half of sausage, oats, beans, most of the nuts and apples, salt, honey.
entries.title: Nuts and apples

entries.reason: Eleven sheets left; I want to know what the first one cost me.
entries.text: Took the first sheet out to look at it in good light at last. Pale and flat all over, as if too much light got in, with a darker band low across it that must be the water. A hundred and twenty with the sun a hand up was too long; I counted for dusk with the sun still in the hole.
entries.title: Pale

queries: pinhole camera picture came out all white
entries.query: pinhole camera picture came out all white
entries.reason: I have eleven sheets and no wish to waste them the way I wasted the first.
entries.text: The more light the paper gets, the darker it turns in the developer, so a wrong count shows as a sheet gone too far one way. Their cure is cheap: start short and double the count each try until something shows. And the light that gets in goes by the hole's area, not its width.
entries.title: Start short, double

entries.text: Ten, then twenty, then forty, on three clear evenings, each written down. Three sheets for one answer. Not tonight: tonight I just look.
entries.title: Not tonight

entries.text: Started across the stepping stones for the edge and only then saw the small one kneeling at the still pool, six strides off, cords in its hands. Every clack of my clogs went out over the water, and the fish under its stone went like sparks. It looked up at me; I'd walked straight through its supper. I lifted a hand, low, sorry, and it lifted one back, and I went on west softer than I came.
entries.title: Clogs on the stones

entries.reason: A map only holds what I've walked.
entries.text: Counted the paces from the landing stone to the mossy boulder again and set the number by the boulder on the sheet. The west side of the map still has one line on it, the edge.
entries.title: Paces west

entries.text: The sun went into the water clean and orange. No shore, no smoke, no sail. Every evening the same answer, and every evening I come back to ask it.
entries.title: Clean into the water

entries.text: The small one didn't jump up or hide when I came clacking over; it just looked, and lifted its hand. Next time I go west I'll cross further up and leave its fish alone.
entries.title: It just looked

entries.reason: The pool was empty, so the stones cost no one anything.
entries.text: Walked back by one lantern turned low. The small one wasn't at the pool but on its log by its fire, so I took the stones. Halfway over I held the lantern up a hand's height toward it, and it put a hand up into its firelight.
entries.title: Light held up

entries.reason: Fire first, then food, or my fingers won't hold a knife.
entries.text: Pit was cold under the ash. Lit a splinter at the lantern for a thimble of oil, fed it into shavings and two dry middles, and it caught on the second puff.
entries.title: Pit from cold

entries.text: Half a loaf and a thumb of sausage by the fire. Left: a loaf and a half, most of the cheese, a ring and a quarter of sausage, oats, beans, most of the nuts and apples, salt, honey.
entries.title: Supper

entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome on a calm, clear night: swung, settled on its scratch.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: Writing it down tonight saves redoing the arithmetic tomorrow.
entries.text: Wrote the day up on a squared page: first sill corner lapped, shimmed and nailed flat; next lap's shoulder sawn; three-four-five on it once four corners are cut. Box: next clear evening, count ten, then twenty, then forty.
entries.title: Written up

entries.text: Legs are heavy from the walk to the edge and back. No saw tonight; it would only cut crooked. Across the water the small one is crouched at its fire with a stick over the coals, cooking something.
entries.title: Legs gone

entries.text: Twisted an arm's length of stalk cord by the fire for new droppers; the fibers are dry and take the twist easy tonight. Over the water the small one sits on its log with something pale glowing in its lap, the way it does most evenings.
entries.title: Cord by the fire

entries.text: Laid two dry middles on the coals crosswise so air gets under them; they caught without a puff. Woodpile: four old sticks and maybe half the armful of middles.
entries.title: Two middles on

entries.reason: A crayfish in the tin overnight is breakfast.
entries.text: Took one lantern down to the shallows. The bait in the trap is picked to bare shell and the cones are empty; whatever ate it found the way out again. Fresh guts in it at first light.
entries.title: Trap empty

entries.text: Across the water the small one is crouched at its fire, pushing a stone up against the ring with a stick. It looked up when my light came down to the water. I kept to the trap.
entries.title: It looked up

entries.text: Tied two droppers of tonight's cord onto the small toggles with wraps instead of knots, the way that held last time. Slow hands, but they're on.
entries.title: Droppers tied

entries.reason: Everything else gets built on that corner, so it has to be right.
entries.text: Sighted down the lapped corner by lantern: flat, no rock, the nail head sunk. The second corner's cheek is daylight work, then three-four-five.
entries.title: Corner holds

entries.text: The low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered. My legs are done; bed early tonight.
entries.title: No answer

entries.onMind: whether a coal will be there at first light
entries.reason: The woodpile is low and the oil is lower.
entries.text: Raked the ash up over the last coals and pushed the ring stones in instead of feeding it. Twice now I've come home to a cold pit and spent oil on a splinter; tonight I'll see if anything keeps under the ash till morning.
entries.title: Banked

entries.text: The small one's fire is still up across the water, but its log is empty. It goes off into the dark sometimes and comes back.
entries.title: Empty log

entries.text: Carried the lantern under the tarp and turned it down. The small one is back on its log by its fire; I lifted the light a little before I blew it out. No idea if it saw.
entries.title: Lantern in

moves.goal: learn the hammer and the nails on scrap that doesn't matter

moves.doing: reading his maker's two new notes on the tablet on the crate
moves.goal: see what his maker wrote while the sun is up to read by

moves.goal: get a real fire under the tin before he eats, so the oats can boil later

moves.doing: eating bread and cheese from the food bundle by his fire
moves.goal: eat a proper meal for the first time in days, like his maker told him

moves.doing: hammering a blunted nail and a sharp nail side by side into the offcut at the bench
